name: Home Charging Quotation Tool
headline: Turned a confusing EV buying step into a clear conversion path, generating 82 qualified leads in 6 weeks.
roleSummary: Principal UI designer, responsible for interaction design, cross-team alignment, and delivery-ready handoff.
summary: On Renault and Dacia websites, home charging was buried and priced with a single default number. I designed an end-to-end quotation tool that made the offer findable, the pricing understandable, and the next steps actionable.
challenge: EV buyers faced pricing uncertainty around home charging installation, while Renault and Dacia websites did not make the offer easy enough to find or understand. Mobilize Power Solutions needed a more visible, more comprehensible, and more actionable experience.

blocks.content: Installing a home charging station is one of the biggest unknowns in the EV buying journey. On Renault and Dacia websites, users only saw a single default price with no way to understand how their own setup would affect the final cost. Mobilize Power Solutions needed an estimation tool that could reduce uncertainty and generate qualified leads.

blocks.caption: Home Charging Quotation Tool: product selection with real-time pricing, embedded across Renault and Dacia configurators

blocks.content: The project had two UX challenges that needed to be solved in order. A first qualitative study (18 participants, conducted by Affordance) revealed a discoverability problem: only 3 out of 18 users found the Mobilize Power Solutions page on renault.fr unaided. But solving visibility was not enough. Once users reached the tool, prototype testing surfaced a second layer of friction: technical complexity.

The charging offer was buried in the site architecture, disconnected from the EV purchase journey. Only 3 out of 18 users found the Mobilize Power Solutions page unaided. I worked on embedding the tool at five high-intent entry points across renault.fr to solve this.

The quotation tool sat at the intersection of multiple teams within the Mobilize charging ecosystem. Displaying the right pricing, product availability, and eligibility rules required constant alignment with several poles: electrical infrastructure, product catalog, pricing engine, and CRM routing. I co-built the project with these teams, participating in cross-functional syncs to ensure the design reflected real business logic and technical constraints at every step.

This was not a project where I could design in isolation. Every screen decision had downstream implications on data flows, partner integrations, and legal compliance. I learned to treat dependency management as a core part of the design process, not something that happens after the mockups are done.

To solve discoverability, I mapped the Renault website architecture to identify the pages where charging intent was highest. The goal was to embed the quotation tool exactly where users were already thinking about home charging, rather than forcing them to find a buried Mobilize page.

items.label: R5 E-Tech — Solutions recharge
items.value: Dedicated charging page for the flagship EV. Users land here from the vehicle configurator. Added a direct CTA to the estimation tool alongside autonomy and cost simulators.

items.label: R5 E-Tech — Financement & services
items.value: Financing page where users compare leasing options. Embedded a charging installation block ('Votre borne installée à partir de 999€') with a link to the quotation tool, catching users in a purchase-decision mindset.

items.label: Mobilize Power Solutions
items.value: The main MPS page, previously the only entry point. Restructured the product comparison (Prise renforcée / Powerbox / Bidirectional) and added a direct 'Commandez votre borne' CTA.

items.label: E-Tech — Recharge hub
items.value: Cross-model charging hub covering home and on-road charging. Added a 'Mobilize Powerbox' section linking to the estimation tool, bridging generic charging content to the personalized quotation flow.

items.label: E-Tech — Services
items.value: Services overview page with a dedicated 'Estimez votre installation' CTA under the charging section. This page captures users exploring the EV ownership ecosystem beyond the vehicle itself.

blocks.content: Post-launch analytics confirmed the strategy: 90% of tool traffic came from these targeted pages. The three highest-performing entry points (MPS page at 41%, E-Tech charging hub at 39%, and R5 product page at 10%) accounted for 95% of completed quotations.

blocks.title: The flow was too technical
blocks.text: With discoverability solved, a guerilla test with 14 participants (April 2024) confirmed the second issue. Three specific pain points emerged around technical terminology, product comparison, and pricing transparency. This test became the foundation of the redesign I led.
blocks.caption: The V3 prototype tested in April 2024: all configuration steps visible on a single scrollable page

blocks.content: The guerilla test (14 participants, 30-45 minute sessions, mix of in-person and remote) placed users in a realistic scenario: they had just bought a Megane E-Tech and needed to install a home charging station. Three critical friction points surfaced.

items.label: Monophase vs. triphase
items.value: Only 4 out of 14 users understood the concept before interacting with help. 8 were completely lost.

items.label: Product comparison
items.value: Users consistently failed to understand V2G concepts. The comparison table was perceived as hard to scan.

items.label: Price banner
items.value: 7 out of 14 only partially understood how configuration choices affected the estimate. The price block felt detached from the inputs.

blocks.content: On the positive side, 100% of users successfully chose their vehicle, 12 out of 14 understood the housing type step, and the overall flow was perceived as faster and more intuitive than competitor tools. The structure worked. The content needed rethinking.
Each finding led to a targeted design iteration. I ran a structured before/after cycle, presenting Version A and Version B proposals for stakeholder validation before final sign-off.

blocks.title: Redesigning the solution selection and pricing
blocks.text: The original product selection showed a basic list with detached pricing. Users could not understand how their choices affected the estimate (7 out of 14 only partially understood), and tooltips explaining technical concepts were too small and hard to discover (only 4 out of 14 understood monophase vs. triphase before interaction). I redesigned the entire solution screen: product cards now show images, promotional pricing, and charging times at a glance. Tooltips were replaced with dedicated links opening detailed modals. The price banner was realigned directly with the configuration zone.
blocks.caption: Before: basic product list with detached pricing and small tooltips

blocks.title: From technical jargon to scannable comparison
blocks.text: Users could not parse V2G concepts or the term 'VH bidirectionnel du Groupe Renault'. The expanded card layout made comparison difficult. I redesigned the product presentation as a compact table with chevron selectors to switch between products, replacing the cluttered side-by-side layout with a focused, one-at-a-time comparison on mobile.
blocks.caption: Mobile product comparison: chevron selectors to navigate between charging solutions

blocks.title: After: clear products, visible pricing, accessible details
blocks.text: The redesigned screen presents each charging solution with product images, crossed-out promotional pricing, and key specs (charging time, compatibility). Technical details previously hidden in tiny tooltips are now accessible through explicit links opening full modals. The price updates visibly as users configure their installation, closing the cause-effect gap that blocked half of test participants.
blocks.caption: After: product cards with images, promotional pricing, and modal-based technical details

blocks.title: From dead-end to actionable paths
blocks.text: The tool also needed to handle cases where users could not be served directly, such as co-ownership setups. I designed a routing logic that redirected users toward the right partner (Zeplug for co-ownership) with clear context, replacing the previous dead-end with a relevant continuation.
blocks.caption: Co-ownership routing: contextual partner handoff with Zeplug instead of dead-end

blocks.content: The original flow displayed all configuration options on a single scrollable page: housing type, electrical setup, vehicle, installation distance, and product selection were all visible at once. Users faced the full complexity upfront, with no sense of progress and no focus. I converted this into a vertical stepper where each step reveals one question at a time, keeping the user concentrated on the current decision. Smooth transitions guide users from one stage to the next, and the contextual image on the left updates to reflect their current selection, reinforcing the sense of progression and keeping the experience grounded in their real situation.

blocks.caption: Desktop prototype: animated vertical stepper with contextual images updating at each step, leading to the lead form

blocks.title: Key screens iterated after user testing
blocks.intro: Each iteration was validated with stakeholders before entering development.
blocks.note: These changes were presented as Version A / Version B proposals for stakeholder sign-off before entering development.

blocks.content: I prepared Figma specifications with a 'Ready for dev' annotation system per component. For each sprint, I created Jira tickets scoped at the component level for Makolab (outsourced development partner), including screen context, interaction notes, state coverage, and links to the relevant Figma frame. After each sprint, I ran Design QA sessions comparing implemented screens against specs.

To streamline the dev handoff process, I co-created a structured handoff template in collaboration with a senior designer on the Renault side. We ran internal workshops to map the team's pain points around design-to-dev handoff, then iterated the template based on real feedback. This template was then adopted as a shared standard across our product teams, reducing QA loops and giving developers a predictable structure for every delivery.

I also introduced a Design QA practice to systematically compare implemented screens against design specs after each sprint. This helped catch visual and interaction regressions early, and the format was later reused on other projects within the team.

blocks.caption: Figma specification page: each screen documented across breakpoints (desktop 1440px, tablet, mobile 375px) with annotated states and interaction notes

blocks.title: Mobile-first approach
blocks.text: Mobile received special attention: product comparison was redesigned as a scrollable card stack, the price banner was repositioned, and installation parameters were reformatted as one question per screen to reduce cognitive load. Desktop (1440px) served as the reference layout.
blocks.caption: Desktop and mobile layouts: same flow, adapted to each context

blocks.content: The tool launched in September 2025 and was embedded across Renault and Dacia EV purchase journeys. Post-launch analytics (Google Analytics + Contentsquare) validated both the product hypothesis and the entry-point strategy.

blocks.title: First 6 weeks after launch
blocks.intro: September 22 to November 6, 2025. Renault brand, France.

items.label: Traffic from the 3 targeted entry points

blocks.content: The 89% completion rate across the first four steps confirmed that the redesigned flow resolved the comprehension issues surfaced in testing. The main drop occurred at step 5 (solution presentation), which correlated with users reaching their goal: a personalized estimate. The tool succeeded as a price discovery engine, even for users who did not convert to leads.

This project reinforced a simple principle: test early, then redesign around the findings, not around assumptions. The guerilla test was not a validation step. It was the starting point of the real design work.

It also showed that reducing technical anxiety is not about removing complexity. Users do not need every concept simplified. They need enough clarity at the right moment to keep moving with confidence.

Working at the intersection of multiple Mobilize teams taught me that dependency management is a design skill. When your screen depends on data from five different poles, the quality of your cross-team communication directly impacts the quality of the final experience.

name: Financing Simulator — Reshape 2026
headline: Redesigning Renault and Dacia's financing simulator to turn an isolated calculator into an integrated conversion tool.
roleSummary: Principal design owner: discovery, redesign, testing, accessibility, prototype creation, and stakeholder alignment across business, legal, and engineering.
summary: The financing simulator worked once reached, but was hard to find, too rigid in its parameters, and too weak at guiding users from simulation to action. I led the redesign across discovery, prototyping, accessibility, and multi-country validation.
challenge: The financing simulator was useful once reached, but too hard to find, too rigid in its parameter model, and too weak at helping users move from simulation to action across a multi-country context.

blocks.content: Renault and Dacia's financing simulator helped users estimate monthly payments, but it was disconnected from the rest of the purchase journey. Users who reached it often dropped off before acting. Users who never reached it missed the financing options entirely.

I led the redesign end-to-end: discovery research, prototype creation, accessibility audit, design system extension, user testing, and stakeholder alignment across business, legal, and engineering. The project spans multiple countries and brands.

blocks.quote: This project is ongoing. This case study focuses on the process, decisions, and methodology rather than final deliverables.

blocks.content: I owned the design plan for this project, defining the approach from discovery through delivery. I collaborated closely with a fellow designer to evaluate design options and challenge assumptions together, ensuring the strategy was robust before committing to a direction. This collaborative planning phase included mapping user journeys, benchmarking competitor simulators, and aligning on the right level of ambition for the MVP.

I also mentored the team on structured test methodology, writing the full test protocol and evaluation grid that could be reused on future projects. The user test results will inform a potential pivot in the product direction, which is still under discussion with stakeholders.

blocks.title: What the first research round revealed

blocks.content: The first discovery test made one thing clear: users valued financing, but the simulator failed to meet them where they were. Three problems surfaced repeatedly.

blocks.title: Core problems identified
items: Discoverability: the simulator was buried inside the configurator. Users with clear financing intent rarely found it.
Comprehension: parameters were dense, price evolution was hard to follow, and optional services were poorly distinguished from the core offer.
Conversion: after simulating, users hit a dead end. The action hierarchy was weak, wording was unclear, and the path to commitment did not build confidence.

blocks.content: I structured the redesign around four levers, each addressing a specific research insight.

blocks.title: Key design changes
items: Compact components: reduced visual density so the experience feels lighter while keeping all necessary information accessible.
Sticky price feedback: the monthly payment remains visible as users adjust parameters, making the link between choices and cost immediate.
Stronger action hierarchy: primary CTAs were given more visibility, and wording was tested to support conversion without feeling pushy.
Modular architecture: the simulator evolved from a standalone page to embeddable components, dedicated per-vehicle financing pages, and a structure adaptable to different market configurations.

blocks.content: I structured the work into three ambition levels (MVP, target, stretch) and built a responsive multi-version prototype close to production fidelity. This allowed comparison between layout approaches and grounded decisions in observed user behavior rather than assumptions.

I ran a moderated user test on UserTesting.com. I wrote the full test protocol, defined the task scenarios, and built a structured evaluation grid to ensure consistent analysis across sessions. The moderated format was chosen deliberately: financing is a high-stakes, high-complexity topic where observing hesitation, confusion, and spontaneous questions matters as much as task completion.

blocks.title: Test methodology
items: Moderated sessions on UserTesting.com with real users
Custom test protocol with scenario-based tasks
Structured evaluation grid for consistent cross-session analysis
Prototype tested at near-production fidelity (responsive, real data)

blocks.content: The initial sessions validated the overall redesign direction but surfaced specific friction points. Three patterns stood out consistently across participants.

blocks.title: Key insights so far
items: Users confused optional services with mandatory fees. The visual separation between what is included and what is added needs to be much stronger.
The price breakdown was trusted but not fully understood. Users need to see the delta between options, not just the final number.
Several users hesitated at the final CTA because the commitment level was ambiguous. The wording needs to explicitly clarify what happens next.

blocks.content: The full restitution and prioritized iteration plan are currently being finalized. The next step is to share findings with stakeholders, align on which fixes enter the MVP scope, and iterate the prototype before a second validation round.

Accessibility was not treated as a final check. It shaped decisions from the start: component selection, interaction patterns, color contrast, and content hierarchy were all designed with WCAG compliance as a baseline, not an afterthought.

I built a dedicated accessibility audit workflow using an internal AI agent to accelerate reviews. The audit restitution template I created for this project has since been adopted by other product teams within the organization as their standard accessibility reporting format.

blocks.title: Accessibility scope
items: Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit on every component before handoff
Keyboard navigation and screen reader compatibility validated
Color contrast verified across both Renault and Dacia brand tokens
Audit restitution template created and reused across teams
AI-assisted audit workflow reducing review time significantly

blocks.content: The simulator required components that did not exist in the current design system. Rather than creating one-off solutions, I extended the system with multibrand elements built on the constructor site tokens.

This included financing-specific patterns (price breakdown cards, parameter sliders, comparison tables) designed to work across Renault and Dacia brand contexts while maintaining the modularity needed for multi-country deployment. Each component was documented with usage guidelines and accessibility specifications.

I used AI intentionally at specific points in the process: generating realistic data sets for prototype fidelity, automating repetitive accessibility audit steps, and accelerating responsive design variations. The goal was never to replace product thinking, but to compress execution time on mechanical tasks while keeping full rigor on strategic decisions.

The moderated user test is complete and the restitution is being finalized. Next steps are sharing findings with stakeholders, aligning on which fixes enter the MVP scope, and iterating the prototype before a second validation round. In parallel, I am collaborating with the site-owner team to improve simulator discoverability through better CTA placement on vehicle pages.

blocks.title: Delivered so far
items: End-to-end responsive prototype at near-production fidelity
Moderated user test completed with structured protocol and evaluation grid
Multibrand design system extension with documented components
Full WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility audit with reusable restitution template
Accessibility audit template adopted by other product teams

blocks.content: This project reinforced how the real work of product design happens at the intersection of usability, conversion, legal review, and multi-country logistics. The design is one layer in a much larger alignment challenge, and owning that complexity is what makes the role senior.

It also confirmed the value of treating accessibility and design system work as integrated parts of the design process rather than separate tracks. When they are woven into every decision, they accelerate rather than slow down delivery.

name: MyPowerbox - Mobile app MV
headline: Launched Mobilize's first mobile app around a connected charging product, from blank screen to app stores.
roleSummary: UI owner and UX co-lead. End-to-end from prototyping through brand alignment, user testing, and design system foundations.
summary: Designing the first official Mobilize mobile experience meant shaping a young brand's digital identity while solving the real UX challenges of a hardware-dependent product with pairing friction and limited budget.
challenge: Designing one of the first official Mobilize mobile experiences meant turning a technically constrained charging-station product into a clear day-to-day app, while shaping an emerging brand with limited budget and white-label ambitions.

blocks.content: MyPowerbox is a connected home-charging station by Mobilize. The app needed to let users pair the device, monitor charging sessions, and manage their energy consumption daily. But this was also Mobilize's first official mobile product, which meant the interface would define how users perceived the brand.

The challenge was threefold: turn hardware constraints into a usable daily experience, shape an emerging brand with limited budget, and build a foundation that could support white-label B2B ambitions later.

blocks.caption: MyPowerbox app: home screen and charging session view

blocks.content: A guerrilla test on the MVP prototype revealed six concrete usability problems. The most critical was the pairing flow between the charging station and the app, the highest-friction area in the entire experience.

blocks.title: The physical-digital gap
blocks.text: Because the experience depended on a physical product, technical constraints from Bluetooth, Wi-Fi provisioning, and firmware updates created friction that could not be solved through UI alone. The UX had to absorb real-world delays and failure states.
blocks.caption: Pairing flow friction points

blocks.title: Setup-centric, not daily-use
blocks.text: The original app structure was built around initial setup. Once pairing was done, users had no compelling reason to return. The navigation did not support the daily actions that would make the app sticky.
blocks.caption: Original navigation model

blocks.title: A daily-use navigation model
blocks.text: I restructured navigation around recurring daily actions: checking charging status, reviewing energy consumption, adjusting schedules. The app became a utility, not just a setup companion.
blocks.caption: Redesigned navigation structure

blocks.title: Guided pairing with stronger feedback
blocks.text: I iterated the pairing flow multiple times with progressive guidance, clearer error states, and visual feedback for each step. The goal was to build confidence during a technically fragile process.
blocks.caption: Redesigned pairing flow

blocks.title: Lottie and Rive animations for credibility
blocks.text: I crafted animations in Figma, then reconstructed them with Lottie and Rive for developer integration. These micro-interactions helped bridge waiting states and gave the product a premium feel that the young brand needed.
blocks.caption: Charging ready state with animated ring built in Lottie and Rive

blocks.title: Two personas driving priorities
blocks.text: Design decisions were grounded in two validated personas: the Early Adopter who wanted visibility over connected devices, and the Pragmatic User who just wanted reliable, simple charging. This framing helped resolve feature-priority debates throughout the project.
blocks.caption: Persona-driven design decisions

blocks.content: I built the first component library for Mobilize mobile apps and documented behavior through interactive prototypes. This was not a theoretical exercise: the library was built alongside the product, validated through development, and designed to be extended by future projects.

The system included color tokens aligned with Mobilize brand guidelines, typography scales for mobile readability, component states covering the hardware-specific edge cases (offline, pairing, firmware update), and motion principles that could be reused across the ecosystem.

blocks.caption: Mobilize mobile design system: component library and documentation

blocks.content: The MVP launched on iOS and Android app stores and was validated through testing. Beyond the release, the project created a reusable base for Mobilize's mobile products.

blocks.title: Post-launch results
blocks.intro: First 3 months after app store release.

items.label: Pairing success rate on first attempt
Reduction in support tickets related to pairing

blocks.title: Key results
items: App shipped on iOS and Android stores
Design system adopted as foundation for future Mobilize mobile products
White-label B2B architecture validated for partner deployment
Brainwriting workshop format reused across the team

blocks.content: This project taught me how different mobile design becomes when the product is tied to a physical device. The UX is not just about screens; it has to absorb real-world delays, hardware failures, and connectivity issues that no prototype can fully simulate.

It also showed how much responsibility sits inside a first product for a young brand. The interface becomes part of the brand definition. Every interaction pattern, every animation, every error state contributes to how users perceive the company behind the product.

name: Citadel Team - Design System
headline: Built Thales Ercom's first design system to create a shared language between design and development.
roleSummary: Solo owner of the system: foundations, component library, documentation, governance, and collaboration rituals with engineering.
summary: Built Thales Ercom's first design system as a solo designer, establishing a shared vocabulary and component architecture that bridged design and development in a low-maturity, partly remote environment.
challenge: No shared design language or source of truth existed, creating inconsistencies, repeated QA, and friction between design and development when building components in a low-maturity, partly remote environment.

blocks.content: Citadel Team is a secure communication product by Thales Ercom. When I joined, there was no shared design language: the same button existed in four different visual variations, spacing was arbitrary, and every component handoff required lengthy explanation. Development teams had no reliable reference, leading to repeated QA cycles.

I was the sole designer tasked with building the first design system from scratch. The challenge was not only visual: it was organizational. I had to create something that could survive beyond my involvement, in a partly remote team with low design-system maturity.

blocks.title: Systematic inconsistencies found
items: The same input component existed in 4 different visual variations across screens
Button hierarchy was inconsistent: primary and secondary styles were used interchangeably
Spacing was arbitrary, with no shared grid or spacing scale
Color usage was based on individual judgment rather than shared tokens
Developers had no reliable reference to check component behavior, leading to repeated QA cycles

blocks.content: The cost was not just visual inconsistency. It was time: every component handoff required explanation, every QA review required re-verification, and every new screen required re-discussion of decisions that should have been settled.

blocks.caption: DS audit and weekly definition sessions

blocks.title: Tokens that removed guesswork
blocks.text: I defined color tokens, typography scale, spacing system, and elevation rules. These were not abstract design decisions. They were constraints that eliminated daily micro-decisions: which gray to use, how much spacing between elements, what shadow depth to apply.
blocks.caption: Component tracking sheet

blocks.title: A library with clear variants and states
blocks.text: Each component in the Figma library included all its variants (size, type, state), with explicit naming conventions that matched the vocabulary developers used. This reduced the translation gap between design files and implementation.
blocks.caption: ZeroHeight documentation

blocks.content: I documented every component in ZeroHeight not just with visual specs, but with usage guidelines: when to use this component vs. alternatives, what behaviors are expected, what accessibility considerations apply. The documentation served as a shared contract between design and development.

I also created reusable page templates for recurring page types and established a component tracking system to monitor which components were designed, documented, and implemented. Regular follow-up sessions with Product and Tech turned the system from a one-way handoff into a collaborative process.

blocks.title: Key results
items: Raised design and development maturity from near-zero to a structured shared practice
Reduced repeated QA loops by giving developers a reliable source of truth
Improved handoff clarity through documented component behavior and shared vocabulary
System continued evolving after initial release, confirming sustainability
Recommended adoption of Storybook to bridge the remaining gap between design documentation and live implementation

blocks.quote: The most important result was not a component library. It was a shared language between design and development that reduced friction and made product work more predictable.

blocks.content: This project taught me that a design system is only partly a UI problem. It is also an alignment problem, a documentation problem, and a collaboration problem.

Building the first version of a system in a low-maturity environment forced me to think not only about components, but about adoption, language, and team habits. If I did it again, I would push for Storybook integration from the start and establish clearer contribution rules earlier to avoid the system depending on a single person.

name: FleetUI - Web App Design
headline: Designed a B2B SaaS dashboard for Renault Digital, turning complex fleet API data into a clear, actionable interface for enterprise fleet managers.
roleSummary: UX/UI designer in a SAFe project team. Conducted discovery research, heuristic evaluation, user interviews, and owned the UI layer from wireframes to design system.
summary: Fleet managers relied on costly external tools or internal screens built without UX consideration. I led the design effort to create a coherent B2B dashboard platform, from market research and user interviews through to a product-specific design system.
challenge: Fleet managers lacked an affordable, purpose-built tool. Existing options were costly external platforms or internal tools built without UX consideration. The product needed to differentiate in a $15B+ market while reducing Renault's internal expenses.

blocks.content: FleetOS is a project inside Renault Digital delivering APIs and data to fleet managers. I worked on FleetUI, the front-end application displaying fleet data in a structured, user-friendly way. I identified the need for this product after learning that internal tools for fleet management existed but were built without design consideration, while external solutions used by affiliates were costly.

A team was formed to create a Fleet Operations SaaS dashboard, a modern B2B tool addressing fleet managers' needs across Europe. I joined after the first building blocks were laid, working within a SAFe project team alongside a Product Manager, two Product Owners, and two Developers. The stakeholder was Mobilize Financial Services.

blocks.title: Discovery: understanding the market and users

blocks.content: I conducted independent market research to understand the fleet management software landscape. The global market was valued at $15.3B in 2023 with a 12.2% CAGR projected through 2030. Key drivers included demand for real-time data and analytics (40%), safety and compliance focus (30%), and rising fuel costs (20%). This confirmed the strategic opportunity but also the competitive pressure.

Following stakeholder interviews, we defined the core question the product needed to answer: how could we differentiate from fleet management competitors while reducing our own internal expenses? The three values we committed to were availability, reliability, and comfort of management.

I also produced a competitive analysis using Mobbin to identify UX patterns and guidelines that suited the product best. This led to six design principles we adopted: flexibility in tool adaptation, humanized data display, smooth multi-path navigation, purposeful data visualization, dynamic emphasis on key information, and accessible assistance.
I conducted a heuristic evaluation based on Nielsen Norman criteria to map the main issues in the existing product. The problems were not isolated to individual screens. They were systemic.

items.label: Spacing & hierarchy
items.value: Spacings too narrow, lack of prioritization and ordering of information across all views.

items.label: Navigation
items.value: No coherent navigation system. Data organized by source rather than operational workflow.

items.label: Colors & contrast
items.value: Dark mode not recommended for usability cases, lack of identifying colors, insufficient contrast between elements.

items.label: Wording & iconography
items.value: Terminology unclear for end-users. Car icons on the map not homogeneous with design, insufficient information density.

blocks.title: Data by source, not by task
blocks.text: Navigation was organized by data source rather than operational workflow. Fleet managers had to mentally map where information lived instead of following natural task flows.
blocks.caption: Existing navigation structure

blocks.title: Too much data, not enough hierarchy
blocks.text: Tables and maps showed dense telematics data without prioritization. Managers could not scan, filter, or act without being overwhelmed by information that was technically accurate but operationally unusable.
blocks.caption: Events log: existing product state

blocks.title: User interviews with an Italian affiliate

blocks.content: We interviewed four users from an Italian affiliate using a structured test protocol to understand their real workflows and pain points. Three major findings emerged.

items.label: Fragmented ecosystem
items.value: Fleet managers juggled at least 5 tools daily that communicated little or not at all between each other.

items.label: Maintenance blind spot
items.value: Maintenance was a major operational challenge with almost no digital automation in place.

items.label: Wasted data potential
items.value: Data was scattered across systems and its potential was not exploited at any level of the organization.

blocks.content: We presented findings to the product team and identified three strategic opportunities: one tool to aggregate the others, seamless connectivity and predictive maintenance, and empowering users through better data visualization. These became the product pillars guiding all subsequent design decisions.

blocks.title: Task-oriented structure
blocks.text: I restructured navigation to match real operational workflows. Fleet view, asset details, events, and alerts became distinct but connected spaces instead of isolated data dumps. A comprehensive sitemap organized all current and upcoming features by target persona.
blocks.caption: Restructured navigation model

blocks.title: Reusable dashboard components
blocks.text: Rather than treating each screen as a separate design problem, I built a pattern library of dashboard components: data cards, filter bars, map overlays, and detail panels that could be assembled consistently across views.
blocks.caption: Dashboard pattern library

blocks.title: Reduced cognitive load
blocks.text: I redesigned the information hierarchy on tables and maps so managers could scan, filter, and act efficiently. The focus shifted from showing all data to surfacing actionable information first.
blocks.caption: Redesigned fleet map view

blocks.title: Product-specific component layer
blocks.text: I personally managed the entire component library for this product, since its needs were specific and the brand had not yet invested in a pushed design vision. I worked closely with developers to keep track of component development in a dedicated Storybook, preparing for the future migration to the Renault Design System.
blocks.caption: FleetUI design system components

blocks.content: Following the evolution of the Mobilize brand, I worked with the Vision team to understand the new brand intentions. I created a moodboard to concretize the identity direction and started a V2 exploration to evolve the graphic charter toward the new Mobilize guidelines. The goal was to simplify visual codes, remove unnecessary details, and go straight to the point while preparing a smooth migration once the Renault Design System was fully operational.

The project transformed a fragmented internal tool into a coherent B2B dashboard foundation for a $15B+ market. I promoted design thinking methodologies and fostered a more collaborative environment among stakeholders. The established guidelines and SaaS dashboard library aimed to increase the company's design maturity for future dashboard projects.

blocks.title: Key results
items: Unified navigation model adopted across all fleet views
Reusable SaaS dashboard pattern library, a previously underdeveloped area within the company
Product direction validated through market research, user interviews, and stakeholder workshops
Design system with Storybook integration used by development team
Brand evolution roadmap defined with V2 exploration mockups

blocks.content: This project taught me how to work in a complex SAFe environment with many stakeholders, and the need to evangelize design culture to technically oriented teams. Collaborating within a sizable design team operating under agile SAFe offered insights into inter-team constraints and the importance of mapping requirements well in advance.

A key frustration was the company's lack of a user-centric or data-centric approach, making it challenging for the voice of the user to be effectively heard. If I did it again, I would push harder for discovery workshops earlier in the process, as these were elements that were often overlooked by project teams.
